title: Asking for the Whole Plan: Prompt Design Moves Language Models’ Scores on a Clinical-Safety Benchmark More Than Model Choice: An Exploratory Study on the NOHARM v2 Public Cases
content: Objective: To measure how much a structured instruction changes large language models' scores on NOHARM, a specialist-consultation benchmark graded mainly on omissions, which part of the instruction carries the change, and whether the added content is safe. Materials and Methods: Twelve models answered the 30 public NOHARM v2 cases (330 items) uninstructed, and 5 also with an instruction requesting a complete, structured plan. An AI evaluator applied the benchmark's severity-weighted F1. On 2 models, each part of the instruction was tested alone and against a request for 25 recommendations. Model raters and a physician reviewed the added actions. Results: The instruction raised F1 by 0.14 on average [0.09, 0.20] and improved 4 of 5 models, most for the tersest (Grok 4.7, 0.354 to 0.633; GPT-5.6 Terra, 0.678 to 0.853). Three instructed models exceeded the best uninstructed score (0.764). The standard deviation between models halved (0.17 to 0.09). The plan format alone matched the full instruction; the framing alone or 25 recommendations scored lower. Most recovered actions were follow-up and counseling. One model proposed +0.13 [+0.05, +0.23] more specialist-rated harmful options per item; a physician judged 13 of the 43 added options harmful as stated. Discussion: On this benchmark, an uninstructed score reflects how much a model volunteers, not only what it knows. A structured instruction recovered omitted care but added some harmful options. Conclusion: Benchmarks of clinical completeness should report scores under a standard structured instruction beside uninstructed scores, and check what the instruction adds, before models or clinical tools are ranked.
